title: Soviet vacuum-tube engineer's all-inorganic hermetic memory package
idea: Soviet tubes lasted because they held no organics: build the memory-logic package with zero polymers, using a glass core, Cu-Cu hybrid bonds, CVD SiCN/SiO2 gap-fill instead of underfill and mould, and an anodically bonded glass lid filled with dry nitrogen.
why: Underfill and mould Tg (~110-150 C) and moisture creep are what kill packages at 125 C; going inorganic removes that cliff and lets HBM-class stacks qualify for 10 years at 125 C.

title: Turbine-blade internal cooling channels inside HBM spacer layers
idea: Adapted from jet-engine blade cooling: serpentine microchannels are etched into thin silicon spacers placed every few dies and carry pumped dielectric coolant through the stack. Heat leaves from the stack interior instead of conducting up through 16 dies.
why: Thermal limits cap stack height and force 2x refresh above 85 C (fact 3); internal cooling could allow 24-32 high stacks and halve hot refresh.

title: Capillary droplet self-alignment for sub-micron chiplet-to-wafer hybrid bonding
idea: Shift alignment from a multi-million-dollar robot to molecular-scale surface tension: hydrophilic pad patterns plus a water droplet pull each DRAM chiplet into register to <200 nm as the droplet evaporates, then Cu/oxide direct bonding locks it. A coarse +/-10 um pick-and-place is enough because the liquid does the last mile.
why: Cuts hybrid-bonding tool capital ~5-10x and raises throughput ~10x, making 1-2 um pitch DRAM-on-logic affordable for U.S. OSATs (capital intensity, U.S. manufacturability, pJ/bit).

title: XOR-delta page migration between memory tiers
idea: Substitute full-page copies when a hypervisor moves pages between HBM, DDR and CXL tiers with XOR deltas against the stale copy kept in the far tier, sending only cache lines flagged dirty since the last migration.
why: Fact 5: tiering traffic down 60-90% for read-mostly pages, making cheap far memory usable so less HBM is needed.

title: Demoscene procedural memory: store generators, regenerate tensors in base die
idea: Demoscene 4 KB intros generate whole worlds from tiny programs. Store weights and KV as compact generators (PRNG seeds, low-rank factors, codebook indices) and expand them in a small base-die engine on read, so the array and interface move only the recipe.
why: Bits stored and moved per logical access fall ~4-16x depending on compressibility, cutting energy per access and multiplying effective capacity.

title: Sr: strontium-titanate pads give bumpless capacitive memory tiles
idea: Coat face-to-face I/O pads with a ~50 nm SrTiO3 film (k~300) so a DRAM chiplet laid face-down overlapping the logic die edge couples signals capacitively at 5-10 um pitch with no solder; tiles are held by a spring clip and can be re-seated or swapped.
why: HBM bump tax and rework (fact 6): contactless coupling at ~0.1 pJ/bit, no bumps to crack, and upgrade/repair without scrapping packages.

title: Fe: magnetically steered parallel self-assembly of DRAM chiplets
idea: Deposit a patterned soft-magnetic Fe/Ni film on the back of each thinned DRAM chiplet and place an addressable electromagnet array beneath the target logic wafer in a fluid bath; thousands of chiplets settle and orient simultaneously into hybrid-bond sites with sub-um magnetic capture instead of serial pick-and-place.
why: Capital and throughput of die-to-wafer memory-on-logic bonding: from ~2k units/hour serial to >100k dies/hour per tool, cutting assembly cost ~5-10x.

title: Optical weight carousel: one circulating copy feeds sixty-four GPUs
idea: Ideal: model weights exist exactly once in the whole cluster. Closest achievable: stream frozen weights continuously around a WDM fiber loop at ~10 Tb/s so each GPU taps its current layer as it passes, holding only a small double buffer instead of a full weight replica in HBM.
why: Usable supply: 64 data-parallel replicas of a 400 GB model collapse toward one, freeing tens of TB of HBM for KV cache and trading scarce DRAM for cheap fiber and optics.

title: Anodized aluminum oxide film as litho-free vertical interconnect interposer
idea: Combine cookware-style anodization with z-axis interconnect: anodize a 50-100 um aluminum sheet into a rigid self-ordered nanopore template (~10^9 pores/cm2), electroplate Cu into every pore and polish both faces, giving a ceramic film that conducts only vertically and connects any pad above to the pad below with no lithography or plasma.
why: Interposer capital and alignment: wet-only, rare-gas-free memory-on-logic interposer, pitch-agnostic so placement tolerance relaxes; ~10x cheaper than TSV interposers.

title: Au: right-to-reuse rule stops shredding retired server DIMMs
idea: Policy: require hyperscalers and IT-asset recyclers to route retired DDR4/DDR5 server DIMMs through certified re-test and resale before any gold-recovery shredding, with a per-GB reuse tax credit; reused modules drop into existing DDR slots unchanged.
why: Usable memory supply: retired fleet DRAM is a large stranded pool currently destroyed for grams of gold; reuse could add several % of annual bit supply at near-zero capex.

title: Acoustoplasticity: room-temperature ultrasonic bonding of DRAM chiplets on moving webs
idea: Use the Blaha acoustic-softening effect: 40-60 kHz ultrasound softens copper bumps so DRAM chiplets bond to printed Cu-on-polyimide in ~100 ms at room temperature, synchronized with web motion like RFID strap bonding.
why: Assembly capex and thermal budget (fact 6): no reflow ovens or thermocompression bonders; heat-free bonding avoids retention damage; pitch limited to ~30-40 um.

title: Memory lives in the top-of-rack switch, not in servers
idea: Substitute per-server DIMMs with DRAM co-packaged inside the rack switch ASIC module and exposed over existing Ethernet/CXL ports as a shared pool with line-rate atomics; servers keep only small local DRAM.
why: Stranded memory (~20-30% idle in clouds): pooling at the switch cuts DRAM bits purchased by ~15-25%.

title: S: Sb2S3 phase-change photonic crossbar pools memory across accelerators
idea: Use low-loss antimony-sulfide (Sb2S3) phase-change cells on silicon-nitride waveguides as non-volatile 2x2 switches in a 64x64 optical crossbar between accelerators and memory sleds; a route is set by one heater/laser pulse and then holds with zero static power, reassigning memory capacity per job.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: pooling typically recovers 20-40% of stranded provisioned DRAM; zero hold power makes per-job remapping cheap vs electrical switch fabrics.

title: The other way round: 28 nm attention engines beside DDR4 do decode
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: instead of moving the KV cache to the GPU, move the low-arithmetic-intensity attention step to the memory. Memory-rich nodes pair many DDR4 channels with 28 nm attention ASICs that run decode attention in place and return only small output vectors, while the GPU keeps the dense matmuls. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Data movement and HBM demand (facts 5, 6): the KV cache leaves HBM entirely, and only ~1/1000 of the KV bytes cross the network per token.

title: Self-timed delay-insensitive memory links with zero idle power
idea: Worsen: keep PLLs, DLLs and termination burning power while the link idles. Flip: use dual-rail or level-encoded self-timed signaling on short interposer links where each transfer is acknowledged by a handshake, so there is no clock tree, no training and near-zero power when no data moves.
why: Average link energy at real utilization (links idle 50-80% of the time): 2-4x lower; removes DLL/PLL periphery area.

title: Local quality: LCD-line glass interposers with zoned fine-line RDL
idea: TRIZ #3 Local quality: run idle Gen-4/5 LCD TFT lines (1.5-3 um lithography on 730x920 mm glass) to make multilayer Cu RDL glass interposers. Fine lines go only in the memory-to-compute shoreline zones and coarse power planes everywhere else, and a-Si/IGZO TFT switches are built in as lane-repair multiplexers. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capital and the CoWoS interposer chokepoint: ~10x more area per pass than a 300 mm wafer and ~3-5x lower interposer cost per mm2, and lane repair raises assembly yield.

title: Phone-PMIC embedded die: DRAM inside the substrate under GPU
idea: Phones embed PMICs and passives inside the PCB core to save height. Embed thinned DRAM dies in cavities of the accelerator's organic substrate directly beneath the GPU, connected by laser-drilled microvias to the GPU's bottom bumps.
why: Memory moves from the beachfront to under the die (~200 um wires) with no silicon interposer; frees GPU perimeter and sidesteps CoWoS capacity limits.

title: Socketed HBM-class modules that outlive three GPU generations
idea: Worsen: solder memory to the GPU so it is scrapped whenever compute retires after 3-4 years. Flip: mount HBM stacks on a compression-mount, fine-pitch land-grid module beside the processor on a glass substrate, so memory is reused across accelerator generations and later redeployed into CXL expanders.
why: Usable supply: 2-3x memory service life means far fewer new bits needed per year and creates a secondary HBM market.

title: Laser in the host, mirror in the memory: optical backscatter
idea: Reverse who emits light: the accelerator package holds the only laser and sends continuous-wave light to each DRAM stack, where reflective electro-absorption modulators on the base die encode read data onto the returning beam, like RFID backscatter. The DRAM side has no laser, no transmitter thermal tuning and no high-power driver.
why: Data-movement energy and reach (fact 5): DRAM-side link energy ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit, and memory can sit 10-100 cm away so capacity is no longer capped by HBM beachfront; the hot memory stack is free of laser-reliability problems.

title: Sunflower phyllotaxis layout: golden-angle memory placement on glass panels
idea: On a large glass-panel substrate, memory chiplets are placed around the accelerator at golden-angle (137.5 degree) spiral positions like sunflower seeds. That gives the densest uniform packing at growing radius, spreads heat evenly, and makes wire length to the nth chiplet grow only as sqrt(n).
why: Data movement and capacity per accelerator: breaks the 6-8-stack edge (shoreline) limit; 2-3x more memory chiplets within a fixed wire-length budget on cheap panels.

title: 2050 engineer's memory utility: optical DDR pools metered like electricity
idea: In 2050 memory is a metered utility: put commodity DDR dies on co-packaged optical chiplets in a memory sled 1-2 m away and reach it over WDM links at ~1 pJ/bit and ~20 ns of flight time, which replaces most HBM with cheap DRAM shared by many accelerators.
why: Escapes HBM's 3x area/bit and TSV yield loss: claimed 2-3x cheaper bits for capacity-bound AI workloads, plus pooling that cuts stranded memory 25%+.

title: Watchmaker's jewel registration: kinematic self-aligned fine-pitch die stacking
idea: Watchmakers seat parts on jewels and pins: etch V-pyramids and pits into the mating die faces and drop in silica micro-spheres so dies self-register kinematically to <200 nm, which allows 1 um hybrid-bond pitch with cheap pick-and-place tools instead of $5M+ bonders.
why: Cuts the capital intensity of advanced stacking while raising bond density 10x, so more memory bandwidth and dies per stack come from cheaper U.S. OSAT lines.

title: MiG-25 engineer: coarse-pitch mature-node 150 C memory interface
idea: The MiG-25 beat titanium jets with robust steel and tubes: define a 150 C-rated memory chiplet interface using 40 um copper pillars and a 28-65 nm base die built in existing U.S. mature fabs, accepting a bit more energy per bit in return for huge margins.
why: Opens automotive and industrial memory supply to U.S. mature-node fabs and OSATs, with no EUV, and frees leading-edge capacity for AI.

title: Photonic wire bonds written after chips are placed
idea: Reverse align-then-place: place memory-side and host-side photonic dies coarsely (+-10 um), image their couplers, and write freeform polymer waveguides between them by two-photon lithography, so the link adapts to placement error rather than demanding sub-micron alignment.
why: Optical memory links (fact 5) without active alignment, a dominant cost of co-packaged optics; university fabs with two-photon writers can prototype memory-disaggregation links.

title: Latching NEMS relay tiles: bits held by mechanical contact
idea: Ideal: a bit held forever with zero leakage, by geometry instead of charge. Closest achievable: a chiplet of nanoelectromechanical relays with adhesion-latched bistable cantilevers in vacuum-sealed wafer-level cavities, written by a 1-3 V pulse and read by contact resistance in ~10 ns, bonded under the GPU as a static scratchpad.
why: Zero refresh and zero standby leakage, no capacitor (fact 1) and no access-transistor tail (fact 3); buildable in mature U.S. MEMS fabs, though contact endurance is the open risk.

title: Sense-amp XOR delta encoding transmits only flipped bits
idea: Box: DRAM x standard x SA with XOR against a shadow latch holding the last-sent word x transition-coded TSVs x Si x standard. Each column remembers what it last sent; the SA outputs the XOR so a wire toggles only when a bit changed, and the receiver re-integrates.
why: Data movement energy: switching activity on correlated AI tensor streams falls 40-60%, cutting TSV and interposer I/O energy proportionally.

title: Double-sided glass interposer: memory below, compute above
idea: Flip the interposer into a sandwich: make through-glass vias in photostructurable glass by UV exposure, bake and HF etch, bond DRAM dies to the underside and compute to the top directly above them, so the memory path is a 100-200 um vertical via instead of millimetres of lateral wire.
why: Facts 5 and 6: lateral interposer wires become short verticals (~0.2 pJ/bit), and glass is cheaper than a silicon interposer and needs only basic litho and wet etch.

title: Sixteen-high hybrid-bonded SRAM cube in the HBM footprint
idea: Worsen: accept that SRAM is too sparse to matter. Flip: thin 16 mature-node SRAM dies to ~20 um and hybrid-bond them face-to-back at ~1 um pitch with dense through-vias, so a cube in the HBM footprint holds ~1-2 GB of nanosecond, refresh-free memory.
why: Capacity tier without capacitors: ~2 GB at ~0.1 pJ/bit and 5-10x lower latency than HBM, buildable in mature U.S. fabs.

title: Cloud billing per byte crossing the HBM interface
idea: Po: moving data costs money, storing it is free. Cloud providers meter and price bytes crossing each accelerator's memory interface and refund locality-friendly jobs, steering frameworks toward fusion and on-chip reuse so fleets need fewer HBM stacks.
why: Software-driven traffic cuts of 20-40% let the same DRAM supply serve more workloads; a market fix for a supply squeeze.

title: Williams-tube revival: electron beams cross a vacuum gap between dies
idea: Revive the CRT storage tube's beam principle with on-chip field-emitter arrays (Spindt or CNT tips) on the memory die firing modulated electron beams across a sealed 5-20 um vacuum gap onto collector pads on the facing logic die, with no metallurgical bond.
why: Fact 6: ballistic transport into tiny collector capacitance with no TSV or bump, potentially >100 GHz per channel, and stacks become reworkable; vacuum sealing and emitter lifetime are speculative.

title: Firmware-defined PHY: one memory stack sold into any standard
idea: Invert 'a DRAM's interface is frozen at tapeout': give the base die a reconfigurable PHY that firmware sets to DDR5, LPDDR5X, wide HBM-like or UCIe/CXL modes, so one stack ships into whichever market is shortest.
why: Inventory fungibility during a 4x price spike: bits flow to the scarcest segment without new tape-outs; fewer mask sets and less SKU risk.

title: Fiber-loop weight carousel stores model weights as light in flight
idea: Worsen: park every weight in a leaky capacitor and drag it across a bus each token. Flip: inference reads all weights in the same order every token, so keep them circulating in a 64-wavelength fiber loop with in-line amplification and periodic electronic regeneration (a 100 km loop holds ~0.8 GB); accelerators tap each layer as it passes.
why: No capacitor or refresh for streaming weights; capacity scales with cheap fiber length instead of wafers, and latency equals loop period (~0.5 ms), acceptable for per-token weight streaming.

title: Interference-lithography buses: the memory bus is a grating
idea: Invert 'interconnect needs mask-based photolithography': memory buses are thousands of identical parallel lines, so pattern them with maskless two-beam laser interference lithography (U.S.-buildable tool), then cut and connect line ends with coarse lithography.
why: Sub-micron bus pitch on interposers without masks or scanners; very low capital and fully U.S. tooling.

title: Water-droplet self-assembly replaces precision pick-and-place
idea: Substitute the $1-3M precision die bonder with capillary self-alignment: hydrophilic bond sites inside hydrophobic surroundings are patterned on interposer and dies, and a dispensed water droplet pulls each roughly placed die into sub-micron alignment as it evaporates before direct bonding.
why: Capital intensity: alignment tooling ~100x cheaper; coarse, parallel placement raises throughput for a small line.

title: Backside signal highway on the DRAM die
idea: Reverse backside power delivery: after thinning, put thick low-RC copper on the DRAM die backside for the global data and command buses, connected by nano-TSVs to each bank's local I/O, which frees front-side metal for array wiring and shrinks the periphery's routing channels.
why: Facts 5 and 7: on-die global data-line energy, a large slice of the 3-4 pJ/bit, drops 2-3x on thick wires, and periphery routing area falls ~10%.

title: Child's floor carpet: TSV-free edge-bonded planar memory tiling
idea: As a child asks 'why stack the blocks when the floor is empty?': tile plain, TSV-free DRAM dies edge-to-edge in a ring around the accelerator on a glass panel and join neighbours by sidewall hybrid bonds at 2 um pitch on the polished die edges, forming a planar 'memory carpet' with die-to-die relay links.
why: Kills the HBM TSV tax (~3x wafer area/bit, 20-30% stack yield loss): commodity-like dies with no TSV keep-out, claimed ~2x bits per wafer versus HBM at ~70% of its bandwidth.

title: Beveled-sidewall printed wiring replaces TSVs in memory stacks
idea: Worsen: drill thousands of TSVs per die so each via eats area and yield. Flip: stack thinned dies in a slight staircase with beveled edges and laser-direct-write or aerosol-jet-print the vertical bus down the sidewalls, so no die area goes to TSVs or keep-out zones.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): recovers ~5-10% of die area and removes TSV-related yield loss; uses OSAT-class tools. Edge-limited wire count caps bandwidth per stack.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM carpet bonded beneath a wafer-scale accelerator
idea: Jump from die stacks to whole wafers: hybrid-bond an entire 300 mm DRAM wafer face-to-face under a wafer-scale logic wafer at 2 um pitch, so every compute tile owns the ~50 mm2 of DRAM directly beneath it through millions of vertical links. Dead DRAM tiles are fused out by a wafer-level map and the tile above borrows its neighbor's memory over the on-wafer mesh.
why: Deletes HBM TSVs, interposer and PHYs (facts 5, 6): vertical hops at ~0.05 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit, and DRAM area per bit returns to DDR5-like with no 3x TSV tax.

title: Import known-good wafers, stack in America on open base die
idea: Scarcity: the U.S. has 1-2% of DRAM wafer capacity. Buy commodity DRAM wafers from any vendor under a wafer-level KGD spec, then do the high-value steps (thinning, hybrid bonding, a vendor-neutral base die from a U.S. logic foundry, final test) in U.S. OSATs.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: captures HBM value-add (~3-5x DDR $/bit) with ~$1-3B of packaging capex instead of a $15B fab.

title: Laser-debonded HBM reclaimed from retired accelerators and remounted
idea: Box: used HBM3 stacks x existing x existing x laser debond, laser solder-jet re-bump, remount on new carrier x reclaimed package x dry laser rework. Retired GPU modules have their HBM stacks lifted by IR laser heating, tested, re-balled with jetted solder spheres and reused on inference cards.
why: Water: a reused stack needs zero fab water (vs thousands of litres per wafer), >100x cut per reused GB; adds supply with no new wafers.

title: Spider-silk droplet bumping: Rayleigh-Plateau instability forms mask-free solder bumps
idea: Spider capture threads bead into evenly spaced glue droplets by Rayleigh-Plateau instability. A thin liquid-metal or solder line is printed along each pad row on a glass substrate and left to break up, with patterned pad wettability pinning exactly one droplet per pad at a pitch set by the line diameter.
why: Capital intensity: bumping without photomasks, plating lines or silicon wafers, aiming at 10-20 um-pitch bumps on glass panels for memory chiplets at very low cost.

title: Flyover twinax cables replace motherboard memory traces
idea: Substitute long PCB memory traces with ultra-low-loss twinax cables terminated right beside the CPU socket, so memory modules sit in a separate sled and each channel supports more DIMMs or longer reach without retimers.
why: Capacity per socket: ~2x DIMMs per channel or memory moved to cooler zones; a small team builds the harness and adapter boards.

title: Displacement current: printed high-k nanocomposite pinless capacitive memory connectors
idea: Print a BaTiO3-polymer high-k layer over connector pads on module and motherboard flex so signals couple capacitively across a thin gap with no metal contact, decoded by pulse-mode receivers; modules slide in with no pins to wear or corrode.
why: Module cost and signal integrity (fact 5): removes stubs and pin capacitance, enabling cheap hot-swap memory expansion; DC power still needs contacts.

title: Rare-gas content ledger in packaging PDKs and CHIPS grants
idea: Combine the packaging process-design kit with a per-step bill of gases: each OSAT/fab step declares its He/Ne/Ar/Kr/Xe consumption, EDA flows total it per product, and CHIPS-style packaging grants pay a per-stack bonus for products built on rare-gas-free flows.
why: Scarce-resource intensity and resilience: makes rare-gas exposure visible and pays for substitution across U.S. memory packaging, hedging Qatar-type outages.

title: Hollerith tabulator revival: spring pins in low-melt cups socket HBM
idea: Revive Hollerith's 1890 tabulator contacts, pins dipping through holes into mercury cups, with Field's-metal (Bi-In-Sn, 62 C melt) micro-cups on the substrate that receive HBM stack pins, making stacks socketed, flux-free and reworkable.
why: Constraint: no fluorinated no-clean fluxes or fluoropolymer underfill; one bad HBM stack is swapped instead of scrapping a $10k+ module (fact 6 yield), raising effective HBM supply ~5-10%.

title: Active interposer merging HBM base dies with GPU memory controllers
idea: Combine the HBM logic base die and the GPU-side memory controller/PHY into one active interposer in a 12-16 nm logic node: DRAM core stacks bond directly onto it with controllers right underneath, so both ends of the PHY pair vanish and the GPU reaches memory over on-chip-style wires.
why: Data movement and GPU beachfront: removes ~1-1.5 pJ/bit of the 3-4 pJ/bit HBM cost and ~10% of GPU die area spent on PHYs/controllers.

title: Another dimension: DRAM dies standing on edge, bonded at sidewalls
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: stand thinned DRAM dies upright like books on a logic base die. Route metal lines to the diced edge and open them as sidewall pads, then solder or hybrid-bond each die's edge to the base, so there are no TSVs and every die has its own path down.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV area and no 12-hop stacking yield cascade, attacking the ~3x area-per-bit penalty, and heat leaves along each die's full height.

title: Fab-reject partial-good DRAM dies stitched by remapping base die
idea: Dies that fail one bank, speed bin or retention test are scrapped even though >90% of their cells work. Buy them at scrap price, stack 8-16 on a cheap logic base die that self-tests at boot and remaps at 1 KB granularity around bad regions, and sell the result as a slower seconds-grade memory tier.
why: Die cost near zero, package plus base die ~$0.1-0.3/GB, ~30-100x below 2026 contract DRAM; trades speed and density; supply ~5-10% of output.

title: Irvine-style edge-metallized die cubes replace TSVs in memory stacks
idea: 1990s military/space 'cube' memories laminated thinned dies and wired them along a ground, metallized side face. Stack 16-32 thinned DRAM dies with edge-routed RDL fans, polish and metallize the cube face at ~10 um pitch, then turn the cube on its side and hybrid-bond that face to a logic base die or interposer.
why: Eliminates TSV keep-out area, TSV etch/fill tools and TSV yield loss (behind HBM's ~3x area per bit and 20-30% yield hit); dies can be near-standard DDR dies with an edge RDL.

title: Virtual Channel SDRAM revived: sector caches and sub-row activation in base die
idea: NEC's VC-SDRAM put SRAM channel buffers in each DRAM to cut row conflicts, but died because its 3-5% die-area cost was too much for a commodity part and controllers ignored it. In HBM/CXL stacks the logic base die offers cheap area: give it per-bank 64 B sector caches and drive segmented wordlines so only the 1/8 row segment holding the requested sector activates, returning sectors instead of whole pages.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): 8x fewer cells activated per random access, cutting the ~5.9 pJ per useful bit by ~3-5x, and fewer full-row activations ease row hammer (fact 9).

title: Knitted micro-spring interposer layer absorbing warpage
idea: Knit 10 um copper-alloy wire into a loop fabric; each loop becomes a compliant vertical spring contact between a giant panel interposer and the board. The knit soaks up thermal-expansion mismatch.
why: Warpage limits package size; compliant knit lets >100 cm2 memory-plus-compute panels survive, putting far more DRAM within short reach.

title: Procedural weights: generator at the interposer synthesizes tensors from seeds
idea: Ideal: weights that take no storage because they are computed on demand. Closest achievable: train models whose weight matrices are a small stored core plus pseudo-random projections regenerated at line rate by a hash/PRNG engine in the base die or interposer, so only seeds and cores (~5-10% of bits) live in static storage.
why: Zero refresh because the stored state fits in SRAM or ROM, and 10-20x fewer bits moved; trades abundant logic for scarce DRAM capacity and bandwidth.

title: Mandated e-waste DRAM harvest re-hosted behind CXL adapter chiplets
idea: Millions of working DDR4 DIMMs from retired servers are shredded yearly, and their manufacturing cost is already sunk. A procurement/ITAD rule requires federally funded and hyperscale decommissions to route DIMMs to re-hosting, where a CXL card with a protocol-translation chiplet, strong ECC and per-chip retirement masks pools 32-64 old DIMMs as a far-memory tier.
why: Bits cost only test plus adapter (~$0.05-0.2/GB), ~50-100x below 2026 contract DRAM; trades energy, density and bandwidth; supply bounded by decommission flow.

title: Glass-panel interposers break the silicon-interposer packaging bottleneck
idea: Worsen: make every HBM attach depend on a reticle-stitched silicon interposer from one supplier's line. Flip: build interposers on 510x515 mm glass panels with 2 um semi-additive copper lines and laser through-glass vias, giving ~8x more interposer area per panel than a 300 mm wafer and a lower-loss dielectric.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: ~3-5x lower cost per interposer mm^2, lower insertion loss trims pJ/bit; panel and PCB supply chains exist in the U.S. and allies.

title: Sense amps on the host: bitline-pitch bonding across dies
idea: Rearrange array and periphery: the DRAM die carries only cell arrays whose bitline segments end in hybrid-bond pads, and sense amplifiers, decoders and I/O live on a logic-process die bonded below at ~1 um pitch. The DRAM process loses its periphery steps, and fast logic transistors sense at lower voltage.
why: Fact 7 (periphery ~49% of die): the array die gets nearly 2x bits per mm2; logic-node sense amps lower VARY and energy (fact 10); one logic die can serve two array dies.

title: Single-flux-quantum superconducting interposer for cryogenic memory links
idea: An SFQ pulse costs Ic*Phi0 ~ 2e-19 J, about 10^4 below CMOS link energy. For 4 K cryo-AI and quantum-control systems, route memory traffic on passive niobium microstrip lines in the interposer that carry SFQ pulses ballistically without dispersion, with CMOS-to-SFQ converters at the cryo-DRAM edge.
why: aJ-scale data movement with zero resistive loss, and cryo-DRAM needs almost no refresh (facts 5, 3).

title: Cryogenic memory pod linked optically to warm compute
idea: Ideal: charge that never leaks. Closest achievable: immerse DRAM stacks in liquid nitrogen (77 K), where access-transistor leakage falls by orders of magnitude and retention exceeds hours, and connect them to room-temperature GPUs only by optical fiber so no copper heat leak or thermal mismatch crosses the boundary; refresh is disabled.
why: Fact 3: refresh power to zero; cold wires also cut resistive loss and permit ~0.5 V arrays (fact 10), with cryocooler overhead paid only on the small memory heat load.

title: Ultrasound replaces TSVs: GHz acoustic links through thinned stacks
idea: Substitute copper TSVs with ScAlN bulk-acoustic-wave transducers on each die's backside: data rides 5-10 GHz ultrasonic bursts through ~30 um of thinned silicon to a receiving transducer on the die above, so the stack itself becomes an acoustic waveguide. No TSV etch, liner, fill, reveal or keep-out zones.
why: Fact 6 HBM TSV tax: removes signal-TSV area and TSV-related yield loss; claim ~20-30% lower stack cost if per-link energy stays under ~1 pJ/bit.

title: Volume holographic page memory steered by silicon-photonic phased arrays
idea: A hologram stores a megabit page per angle in a cheap photopolymer block and reads it in one flash onto a detector array, so bandwidth comes from page parallelism, not fast cells. Replace slow angle addressing with silicon-photonic optical phased arrays switching in ~100 ns, and hybrid-bond the detector array to an SRAM page buffer.
why: Medium cost could make read-mostly working sets ~100x cheaper per GB; trades write speed, latency and alignment robustness.

title: One via through the whole stack, etched last
idea: Reverse via-first-per-die: adhesive-bond 4-8 thinned dies that each reserve aligned keep-out windows, then DRIE a single hole through the entire stack, line it with parylene and fill copper once, contacting each die through exposed sidewall metal rings.
why: TSV tax and process count (fact 6): one via process instead of one per die and fewer bonded interfaces in the signal path; DRIE plus plating suffices.

title: Aerogel thermal moat between hot logic and memory stack
idea: Ideal: memory stacked on logic yet as cold as if it were far away. Closest achievable: a 20-50 um silica-aerogel or vacuum-gap layer, pierced only by thin copper signal pillars, thermally isolates DRAM tiers from the logic die while a separate cold plate cools the DRAM from its own side.
why: Facts 3 and 5: memory-on-logic normally heats DRAM and doubles refresh per ~10 C; keeping DRAM below ~50 C halves refresh and makes zero-distance stacking practical.

title: SiGe bipolar PHY chiplets deliver fast I/O from mature U.S. fabs
idea: Invert 'fast memory I/O needs leading-edge CMOS': build the memory SerDes/PHY as a separate chiplet in U.S. SiGe BiCMOS (GlobalFoundries Vermont/New York) whose HBTs exceed 300 GHz fT, while DRAM base logic stays on a mature node.
why: 64-112 Gb/s lanes without foreign leading-edge nodes; cheaper base dies and domestic I/O supply.

title: Mantis-shrimp polarization multiplexing in glass waveguide memory links
idea: Mantis shrimp tell linear and circular polarization apart. In the same spirit, ion-exchanged waveguides in a glass interposer carry up to four polarization or polarization-mode channels per wavelength, which polarization-splitting couplers separate at each memory chiplet.
why: Optical I/O density (fact 5): 2-4x channels per waveguide and per laser line, cutting laser count and optical area per Tb/s, built in glass rather than on silicon-photonics wafers.

title: Nephron countercurrent coolant loops through stacked DRAM tiers
idea: Microchannels in alternating DRAM tiers carry coolant in opposite directions, like the loop of Henle, so the hot outlet of one layer sits beside the cold inlet of the next and every die sees nearly the same temperature. The whole stack stays below 85 C, the point where DRAM refresh rate doubles.
why: Refresh (fact 3) and stack height: avoids 2x refresh in hot upper tiers and allows 16-24-high stacks beside 1 kW accelerators; ~10-20% refresh energy and bandwidth recovered.

title: Build the stack top-down on its own SiC heat spreader
idea: Combine the temporary thinning carrier with the final lid: bond the top core-die wafer face-down onto a permanent SiC wafer, thin it, then bond each next wafer face-down onto the previous backside, finishing with the base logic wafer, so the SiC wafer is the carrier for every step and becomes the heat spreader. No temporary bond/debond cycles and no excimer debond lasers (Xe/Kr in neon buffer).
why: Stacking cost, yield and thermal: eliminates N bond/debond cycles per stack and their yield loss, ~2x better top-side heat path (SiC ~370 W/mK), fully rare-gas-free.

title: Flex-wrapped memory: DRAM ribbons folded around the compute package
idea: Invert 'memory sits on a flat plane next to compute': mount thinned DRAM dies on U.S.-made polyimide (Ohio) flex with fine-line wiring and fold it around the four sides and top of the accelerator module.
why: Uses five faces instead of one plane: ~3-4x memory contact perimeter and shorter links than 2.5D in the same footprint.

title: Coulomb blockade: printed gold-nanoparticle films as threshold bus terminations
idea: Print ligand-capped 2-4 nm Au nanoparticle arrays whose collective Coulomb-blockade threshold keeps them insulating for small signals but conducting beyond a size-tuned voltage; as terminations they absorb reflections only during overshoot instead of burning static ODT current.
why: I/O power (fact 5): on-die termination burns a large share of DDR interface power; nonlinear termination could halve it; threshold uniformity is speculative.

title: Optical backscatter pixels: DRAM reflects instead of emitting light
idea: Po: memory that reflects rather than shines. One mask etches micro-cavities in the top dielectric over an existing metal layer used as a mirror; a blanket electro-optic polymer fills them, and the top electrode modulates how much of the lid laser's light each pixel reflects to a detector array.
why: Optical I/O with no laser or photodetector on the DRAM die and one mask; potential ~0.3 pJ/bit and thousands of parallel lanes.

title: Taking out: cold MoE experts moved to router-ahead prefetched DDR4 tier
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out the cold mass: mixture-of-experts models keep only routed-hot experts in HBM, and the rest live in commodity DDR4 behind 28 nm CXL controllers. A tiny predictor runs the next layer's router one layer early so the needed experts stream over CXL before they are used. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Do DRAM's job with less HBM: 2-4x less HBM per accelerator for MoE inference, shifting capacity to cheap trailing-node DRAM.

title: Retina-style monolithic IGZO memory layers grown on glass interposer
idea: The retina builds its photoreceptor, bipolar and ganglion layers in one tissue with the wiring on top. Likewise IGZO gain-cell DRAM tiers are deposited directly on the glass-core interposer beside the GPU site at BEOL temperatures (<400 C), so the memory and its wiring are one monolithic structure with no microbumps, TSVs or separate memory dies.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and data movement (fact 5): GPU-to-memory wires become mm-scale RDL with no PHY crossing; stack yield loss and silicon wafer use for memory disappear.

title: Clamped unbonded die stacks with inductive coupling and swappable layers
idea: Invert 'stacks are permanently bonded': DRAM dies are stacked with no microbumps or TSVs, held by a spring clamp, talking through on-die inductor coils with power fed through edge contacts; a die that fails burn-in is popped out and replaced before final encapsulation.
why: Attacks the HBM TSV tax and 20-30% stack-yield loss: die-level rework turns a scrapped 12-high stack into a one-die swap, and coil area replaces TSV keep-out area.

title: Park KV caches in network-switch SRAM across the rack
idea: Ideal: storage that already exists and sits idle. Closest achievable: modern switch ASICs carry ~100-200 MB of SRAM packet buffer that is mostly empty at moderate load; reserve part of it as a rack-wide static parking lot for KV pages of paused conversations, addressed by RDMA-like verbs and evicted under congestion.
why: Zero refresh power for parked state and new capacity from silicon already deployed (dozens of switches per pod at 100+ MB each), relieving HBM pressure from idle sessions.

title: Mercury-thermometer liquid-metal channels in an elastomer interposer
idea: Like mercury in a thermometer, fill micro-channels in a silicone/polyimide interposer with Ga-In liquid metal at room temperature. The result is stretchable, self-healing, reworkable wiring between memory stacks and compute that tolerates warpage.
why: Removes solder fatigue and warpage failures in large multi-stack packages and allows rework. That makes panel-size modules with more memory possible.

title: Dielectrophoresis: fluidic self-assembly drops memory chiplets onto roll-to-roll interposers
idea: Flow shaped DRAM chiplets in a carrier fluid over a printed polyimide interposer web whose electrodes form dielectrophoretic traps matching the chiplet outline; chiplets lock into sites at tens of thousands per minute, then printed solder joins them.
why: Packaging capex and throughput (facts 4, 6): replaces serial pick-and-place, making many-small-die memory modules (higher die yield) cheap; site-fill yield is the risk.

title: Carousel DRAM: memory broadcasts everything, consumers just listen
idea: Reverse request/response: in carousel mode the DRAM runs a fixed scan that reads every row in order and broadcasts it on a wide unidirectional bus, and consumers (e.g. LLM decode cores that read the same weights in the same order every token) latch what they need. The scan read restores each row, so separate refresh disappears, and there is no command/address bus or random activation; a small conventional port handles writes.
why: Attacks overfetch and refresh (facts 3, 5, 8): 100% row utilisation instead of ~1/128, refresh energy and bandwidth folded into useful reads, CA pins and controller removed; estimated 3-5x lower pJ per useful bit for weight streaming.

title: GPU tensor cores decode memory codewords so the base die stays dumb
idea: Move error correction across scales, from a small base-die ASIC to the accelerator's idle matrix engines: stacks ship raw 1%-BER codewords with parity, and the GPU runs batched min-sum LDPC decoding on tensor cores in the shadow of other loads. The stack's base die can then be built on the DRAM process with no logic node.
why: Lets cells run at 1% BER while removing the costly logic-process base die (fact 6, capital); decoding costs ~1-3% of GPU throughput.

title: Core-memory ferrite rings replace TSVs as fluorine-free inductive stack vias
idea: Revive core memory's transformer coupling: each thinned die carries thin-film coils around sputtered NiZn/NiFe ferrite ring segments aligned through the stack, so flux threads 4-8 dies like wires through a core and carries data with no holes etched.
why: Constraint: removes Bosch DRIE (SF6/C4F8) TSV etch and HF post-cleans entirely; the ferrite core concentrates flux so coils shrink ~3x versus air-core inductive links, raising channel density and cutting the HBM TSV area/yield tax (fact 6).

title: Monolithic gain-cell memory in logic BEOL using dry steps only
idea: Box: 2T0C gain cell x ALD In2O3 channel transistors x current sensing in logic FEOL x monolithic BEOL integration x the logic wafer x ALD, plasma etch and vapor-HF cleans only. Memory layers are deposited above the compute inside its interconnect stack: no separate DRAM wafer, no dicing, no thinning, no package-level memory link.
why: Water: the separate DRAM fab and packaging water disappear and the added BEOL steps are dry, >10x less per GB; data movement drops to ~0.05 pJ/bit.

title: Toothpaste: stencil-printed silver-sinter micro-bumps for chiplet assembly
idea: Squeezed like toothpaste: nano-silver sinter paste is stencil-printed into 40 um-pitch bumps and sintered at about 200 C without thermocompression bonders, on equipment that SMT lines already own.
why: Capital intensity and thermal budget; low-temperature joints protect DRAM retention, and assembly needs about 1/10 the tool cost.

title: Latching phase-change optical switches pool memory at zero hold power
idea: Eliminate the always-on electrical switch in memory pooling: build the rack's memory fabric from GST-clad silicon-photonic switches whose routing state latches non-volatilely, so host-to-memory assignments persist through power loss and cost no energy to hold.
why: Pooling recovers ~20-30% stranded DRAM; latching optics remove switch-ASIC power and post-outage re-discovery, making pooled memory cheaper to run than local.

title: Dynamics: optical circuit-switched rack memory pool from 90 nm photonics
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: build memory-pooling links with silicon photonics from existing 90/45 nm photonics foundry lines, plus a MEMS optical circuit switch that reconnects DRAM sleds to whichever servers need them every few seconds. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Do DRAM's job with less: datacenter DRAM utilization rises from ~50% to ~75-80%, so ~30% less DRAM is bought, and optics keep added latency to ~150 ns across racks.

title: Bell WT4 revival: polyethylene millimeter-wave waveguides carry rack memory traffic
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1970s WT4 millimeter waveguide as HDPE or polystyrene dielectric waveguides (not PTFE) at 130-300 GHz, driven by CMOS mm-wave transceivers on CXL memory sleds and linking pooled memory 1-5 m to compute.
why: Constraint: avoids PTFE dielectric and fluoropolymer cable jackets; ~1-2 pJ/bit and lower cost than optics at rack reach makes memory pooling cheap enough to raise utilization.

title: Railway switch: MEMS optical circuit switching pools rack memory
idea: Like railway points: memory sleds connect over fiber through a MEMS optical circuit switch that re-routes whole sleds to whichever accelerator needs capacity, reconfiguring on ms timescales.
why: Stranded memory (often 20-30% in clusters) becomes usable supply, raising effective DRAM per dollar with no new wafers.

title: Wavelength-addressed rack memory pool with passive grating routers
idea: Po: an address is a colour. Each pooled DRAM module owns a laser wavelength, and a passive arrayed-waveguide grating router connects any accelerator to any module just by tuning its transmitter, so no electronic switch sits in the memory path.
why: Pooling raises usable memory supply 20-40% with no new fabs, at switchless latency and low pJ/bit.

title: Electrochromism: zero-holding-power optical shutters reconfigure rack memory-pool topology
idea: WO3/NiO electrochromic shutters placed in front of a fixed fan-out optical mesh open or close specific memory-to-host light paths; they switch in ~100 ms and hold state with no power, letting a rack reassign terabytes of pooled DRAM between servers as workloads shift.
why: Raises usable memory supply by cutting stranded DRAM (often 20-30% idle per server) with no new bits; slow switching fits allocation timescales.

title: Rack spot market for stranded memory, priced per GB-second
idea: Ideal: no gigabyte sits idle anywhere. Closest achievable: CXL-attached rack memory pools publish idle capacity to a scheduler that leases it per GB-second to neighbouring servers, migrating cold pages at ~10 ms granularity and reclaiming on demand.
why: Usable supply: 25-40% of server DRAM is stranded at any moment; recovering half of it raises effective fleet supply 12-20% without new wafers.

title: Electrolyte 'blood' power delivery replacing HBM power TSVs
idea: A redox-flow electrolyte circulates through microchannels in each DRAM tier, and on-die flow-cell electrodes convert it to the local supply voltage, so the same fluid cools and powers the die as blood carries both oxygen and heat. The power and ground TSVs, the majority of vias in an HBM stack, are removed.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): power/ground TSVs are often >50% of TSVs; removing them saves several % die area, raises stack yield and adds cooling for taller stacks.

title: U.S. stacking hubs: import arrays, add value through hybrid bonding
idea: Ideal: the U.S. gains DRAM capacity without first building a $15B fab. Closest achievable: fund domestic advanced-packaging hubs that buy known-good DRAM wafers from several allied fabs and do thinning, hybrid bonding, base-die attach and test in the U.S., later becoming the integration point for U.S.-made arrays.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: packaging lines cost ~$1-3B and 18-24 months vs 3-5 years for a fab, capture ~40-50% of HBM value, and relieve the stacking-capacity part of the HBM bottleneck.

title: Zinc solders abandoned for corrosion; Zn-Al fluxless joints inside sealed stacks
idea: Sn-Zn and Zn-Al solders were rejected in the 2006 lead-free transition because Zn oxidizes and corrodes in humid, flux-based board assembly. Inside an HBM-style stack the joint is never exposed: deposit Zn-Al eutectic caps on Cu pillars, reflow fluxless in formic-acid vapor and encapsulate immediately in molded underfill, replacing SnAg microbumps and In-based low-temperature solders.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: removes Sn (~2 ppm of the crust, concentrated supply), Ag and In from the microbump layer of every stack; Zn-Al (381 C) also serves as a high-temperature first joint in the solder hierarchy.

title: Display fabs build IGZO gain-cell memory into glass interposers
idea: Worsen: allow only memory fabs with 75:1 capacitor etch to make working memory. Flip: Gen-8.5 display fabs already pattern billions of IGZO TFTs on 2.2x2.5 m glass, so build 3T gain cells (charge held on a read transistor's gate, no capacitor) in the glass interposer's layers, turning the substrate under the chips into seconds-retention memory.
why: Capital and scarce-resource intensity: uses surplus display-fab capacity instead of DRAM fabs; IGZO leakage <1e-19 A/um nearly kills refresh. Density is low (tens to hundreds of MB per interposer).

title: Domain-wall racetrack shift registers in interposer back-end layers
idea: Worsen: give random-access cells to data that is always read in sequence. Flip: deposit magnetic nanowire racetracks in the interposer back-end, where current pulses shift domain walls past one read/write head per track, so weights and activations stream out with no capacitor and no transistor per bit.
why: Density and cost: one access device per hundreds of bits on a BEOL-only process, no refresh; suited to streaming tensors.

title: Origami artist folds one thinned wafer into an accordion stack
idea: Fold rather than stack: process DRAM on a partial wafer thinned to 10 um on a polyimide carrier with continuous RDL running across score lines, then fold it into a zig-zag accordion of 8-16 layers so the inter-layer wiring runs around the folds.
why: No TSVs, no die-to-die bonding and no known-good-die stacking yield multiplication; claimed ~40% lower stacking cost per bit than HBM.

title: Tree-ring rolled memory: spiral-wound foil with metallized edge contacts
idea: A tree adds one ring a year. Oxide-TFT memory film is deposited roll-to-roll on stainless-steel or polyimide foil, wound into a cylinder like a film capacitor, and its bus lines end at one edge that is metal-sprayed (Schoop process) to form thousands of axial contacts to a controller cap.
why: Capital intensity and density: roll-to-roll deposition replaces wafer fabs; one roll packs square meters of memory into a small volume, aimed at capacity tiers below wafer-DRAM cost per bit.

title: Glass-panel substrate memory: multi-tier oxide TFT cells in package RDL
idea: Jump to display-panel scale: the 600 mm glass package substrate is built on LCD lines with 8 tiers of IGZO thin-film-transistor capacitor cells in its redistribution layers, giving a few GB per package of working memory; the ~1% BER from TFT variation is absorbed by row codes in the logic die.
why: Adds non-EUV, U.S.-buildable capacity on LCD-class capital (fact 4) right next to the logic die.

title: Series voltage-stacked DRAM dies eliminate most power TSVs
idea: Eliminate low-voltage high-current power delivery: stack 12 dies electrically in series across a ~13 V rail so each die floats in its own ~1.1 V domain and the same current is recycled through all dies; on-die switched-capacitor balancers absorb mismatch and capacitive level shifters carry data between domains.
why: Power/ground TSVs are a large share of HBM TSVs and IR drop caps stack height; 12x lower current cuts power TSV count up to ~10x, shrinking TSV area tax and enabling taller stacks.

title: Merging: data carriers superimposed on power TSVs
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: about half of HBM TSVs carry only VDD/VSS. Superimpose low-amplitude 10-20 GHz on-off-keyed carriers on them, with on-die LC band-pass taps and notch filters on the decoupling network, so power TSVs also carry data without new holes.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): +30-50% bandwidth per unit of TSV area, or ~25% fewer TSVs for the same bandwidth.
